title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling playbook, benchmarking suite, runbooks
author: Maya Chen
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite guidance, release notes, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is the single reference for engineers operating and evolving Redwood's inference runtime. The intent is to be prescriptive for on-call, actionable for performance tuning, and lightweight enough to use during model onboarding and release planning.

Scope

- Runtime architecture overview and key components
- Kernel scheduling and prioritization policies (GPUTaskScheduler)
- Profiling playbook for latency, tail, and memory regressions
- Benchmarking suite: workloads, metrics, CI integration, and thresholds
- Release notes conventions for runtime releases affecting scheduling/throughput
- Known issues and mitigation patterns
- Runbooks for common incidents and troubleshooting checklist

Runtime architecture (high level)

Summary: The runtime consists of three logical layers: the Frontend (ingest & routing), the Scheduler & Orchestrator (batching, kernel selection, placement), and the Execution Engine (GPU kernels, KV cache management, and quantized runtime).

Components:
- Frontend API Layer
  - HTTP/gRPC ingress, request validation, auth, and routing policy application (region, latency tier, customer tier).
  - Owner: eng-platform/api-ingress
- Scheduler & Orchestrator (GPUTaskScheduler)
  - Responsible for request aggregation, dynamic batching, priority queueing, kernel selection hints, and fallback routing to smaller model variants.
  - Exposes admission-control hooks and metrics: batch_size, queue_time_ms, scheduling_decisions.
  - Owner: eng-serving-runtime/scheduler-team
- Execution Engine
  - GPU process per-device (or per-GPU pool), dynamic kernel loader, quantized kernels (INT8/FP16), KV cache manager with TTL and eviction policies.
  - Integrations: CUDA/cuBLAS/cuDNN, Triton-compatible shim, custom fused attention kernels.
  - Owner: eng-serving-runtime/execution-team
- Observability & Telemetry
  - Token-level tracing, per-route latency breakdown, SLO dashboards, flamegraphs, and perf traces stored in the observability cluster.
  - Owner: eng-platform/observability

Design principles:
- Keep fast-path synchronous and minimal (enqueue -> schedule -> execute).
- Make scheduling decisions deterministic for reproducible perf testing.
- Prefer graceful degradation: fall back to smaller model variants or lower-cost kernels on overload.

Kernel scheduling (GPUTaskScheduler)

Goals: minimize p95/p99 latency while maximizing GPU utilization and respecting customer priorities (tiered SLAs).

Key concepts and data structures:
- Task size: estimated token generation budget (tokens_remaining) and maximum sequence length.
- Priority class: {realtime, standard, background} assigned by routing policy.
- Kernel profile: per-model per-seqlen preferred kernel id, warmup cost, memory footprint, expected throughput.
- Batching window: adaptive (10ms - 70ms) depending on incoming QPS and latency budget.

Scheduling policy (summary):
1. Admission control: reject or route to dedicated pool if queue_time_estimate + expected_exec_time > latency_budget.
2. Prioritized queue: realtime requests are dequeued first; standard requests are batchable across routes; background jobs use spare capacity.
3. Batch formation: group by kernel profile and quantization compatibility, prefer homogeneous batches to enable fused kernels.
4. Kernel selection: pick the kernel variant with best predicted tokens/sec given sequence length and available memory; prefer lower-precision kernels if quality profile allows.
5. Fallback routing: if estimated queue_time exceeds SLO, automatically route to a compatible smaller model variant or degrade to cached response.

Scheduling thresholds (example):
| Metric | Realtime | Standard | Background |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Target p95 latency (inference) | 50ms | 150ms | 500ms |
| Max queue_time_budget | 20ms | 60ms | 300ms |
| Max batch_size | 16 | 64 | 128 |

Admission control rules (examples):
- If predicted_queue_time + predicted_exec_time > request.latency_budget then: a) route to dedicated pool (if available) b) attempt to serve with smaller variant c) return 429 + Retry-After for non-critical customers.

Profiling playbook (run during performance regressions or onboarding)

Objective: quickly triage CPU/GPU hotspots, kernel regressions, and unexpected memory growth. Follow the checklist below in order (fast-to-slow):

1) Validate symptom and scope
  - Reproduce from CI benchmark for affected model and sequence lengths.
  - Confirm whether issue is p50/p95/p99 or memory OOM.

2) Collect lightweight traces (10–60s)
  - nvidia-smi dmon --delay=1 -s u --> GPU utilization, mem usage trends
  - curl -s -D - -o /dev/null http://<endpoint>/health  (check readiness/latency)
  - Runtime metrics: curl to /metrics endpoint (prometheus) and capture batch_size, queue_time_ms, kernel_hint

3) Capture GPU kernel traces
  - NVIDIA Nsight Systems (ncu for micro-profiling):
    - nsys profile --output=trace.nsys --capture-range=cudaProfilerApi --sample=none --trace=cuda --duration=30s --env="CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0" 
    - ncu --target-processes all --set full --export=trace.ncu  ./inference_process
  - Export timeline and inspect: kernel durations, memcpy H2D/D2H, kernel queue stalls.

4) CPU-side flamegraphs and contention
  - perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 30 && perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded && flamegraph.pl out.folded > perf.svg
  - py-spy (Python worker stacks): py-spy record -o profile.svg --pid <pid> --native

5) Memory tracing
  - GPU OOM: capture driver logs (/var/log/nvidia-installer.log) and runtime heap stats exposed by the runtime (/debug/mem).
  - Check KV cache hit ratio and TTL evictions.

6) Kernel-level metrics validation
  - Compare observed kernel variant vs recommended kernel from the kernel profile registry. Mismatches indicate scheduling hints are stale.

7) Regression verification
  - Re-run CI microbenchmarks (see Benchmarking Suite section) and compare baseline. Use p95/p99, tokens/sec and GPU SM occupancy as primary signals.

Checklist for profiling artifacts to attach to an investigation ticket:
- Repro script or CI link
- /metrics snapshot (prometheus export)
- Nsight/NCU trace files (trace.nsys/trace.ncu)
- perf/flamegraph svg files
- kernel_profile lookup for the model and seqlen

Benchmarking suite

Purpose: provide reproducible workloads and baseline numbers for model variants, kernel variants, and quantization profiles. Benchmarks are split into: microbench (single-GPU kernel perf), per-model (small/medium/long sequences), and system (multi-GPU throughput under mixed priority workload).

Workloads included:
- echo-small: short prompts (avg 16 tokens in, 32 tokens out) for high QPS workloads
- chat-medium: conversation-like distribution (avg seq-in 128, gen 256)
- long-lm: long-context generation (seq-in 1024, gen up to 2048)
- embedding-bulk: batched embedding workloads (batch sizes 64-1024)
- stress-mixed: mixed priority traffic with 70% standard / 20% realtime / 10% background

Core metrics collected:
- p50/p95/p99 latency (ms), tokens/sec, GPU_utilization (%), SM_occupancy (%), memory_bytes, batch_size_distribution, kernel_variant, KV_cache_hit_ratio

CI integration and pass/fail thresholds:
- Benchmarks run nightly in a stable hardware lab (CI tag: nightly-perf).
- PR gates: microbench and per-model tests must not regress more than 5% p95 or 10% tokens/sec without an approved performance note.
- Release blocking thresholds:
  - p95 regression > 10% for a primary model on default config -> fail release
  - tokens/sec drop > 15% on quantized kernels -> require rollback or mitigation plan

Running benchmarks locally (example):
- ./benchmarks/run_per_model.sh --model redwood-7b --seqlen 128 --iters 500 --device 0
- ./benchmarks/microbench.sh --kernel fused-attn --batch 16 --device 0

Release notes (runtime releases)

Format conventions for runtime release notes that touch scheduling or kernels:
- Title: runtime v<major>.<minor>.<patch> — summary
- Breaking changes: explicit list and migration steps
- Performance changes: measured deltas (p95/p99, tokens/sec) for representative models and contexts
- Rollout plan: % rollout per stage, primary canary checks, telemetry to watch
- Owners and rollback contact

Example entry:
- runtime v1.14.0 — improved fused-attn kernel and adaptive batching
  - Performance: redwood-7b p95 improved 14% @ seqlen 128 (nightly lab)
  - Rollout: canary 5% -> 25% -> 100% over 48 hours; watch p99 and kernel-mismatch metric
  - Rollback: revert kernel symlink to v1.13.4 and restart gpu-agent on pool nodes

Known issues (operational)

- Issue: Rare p99 spikes when mixing long-context and short-context requests on same GPU pool
  - Symptom: p99 increases by 3x for short requests during sustained long-generation jobs
  - Mitigation: enable per-route isolation (route long-context to dedicated pools) or configure batching_window=small for short routes
- Issue: KV cache memory leak on edge-case tokenization when truncated sequences are accepted
  - Symptom: memory growth over 24–72 hours leading to OOM on small-GPU nodes
  - Mitigation: force periodic kv_cache.compact in nightly maintenance and upgrade kernel that fixes reference counting (runtime v1.13.1+)
- Issue: NCU shows occasional long memcpy H2D on startup of large models (cold load)
  - Symptom: first inference after model load has 10–30x higher latency
  - Mitigation: use prewarm policy: prefetch weights and run a synthetic warmup batch after model load

Runtime runbooks (on-call quick reference)

1) Symptom: Sustained p95 regression across multiple routes
  - Step 1: Check global metrics dashboard -> is meta-metric scheduling_queue_time increasing? (if yes, proceed)
  - Step 2: Identify affected pools: dashboard shows pool_id and impacted nodes
  - Step 3: If queue_time high and GPU utilization < 70%: suspect serialization/lock or host-side bottleneck -> collect perf/flamegraph on scheduler process
  - Step 4: If GPU utilization ~100%: consider scaling out dedicated pools, enable smaller quantized kernel fallback, or temporarily shift background workloads
  - Step 5: If regression caused by recent deploy: roll back to previous runtime/kernel and run postmortem

2) Symptom: OOM on GPU during request processing
  - Step 1: Identify model and node from logs (/var/log/runtime/gpu-<id>.log)
  - Step 2: Capture /debug/mem and kv_cache stats and kill offending worker if it is leaking memory
  - Step 3: If leak persists after restart, set pool.max_models_in_memory = N-1 and schedule node for drain for deeper investigation

3) Symptom: Latency tail for realtime requests
  - Step 1: Verify routing assigned correct priority_class; check policy service
  - Step 2: Ensure batching_window for realtime routes <= 20ms; if not, apply emergency override
  - Step 3: If still occurring, check for kernel-mismatch (requests being scheduled onto non-optimal kernels) and force kernel_profile refresh

Team wiki / ownership and onboarding

- Owners: eng-serving-runtime (primary), eng-platform (observability)
- On-call rotations: serving-runtime team has 2-week rotation, responder roster in Ops on-call calendar
- Onboarding checklist for new team members:
  1. Read this document and serving-runtime-reference-2026-03-04
  2. Run the per-model benchmark locally and reproduce baseline numbers
  3. Shadow on-call playbook for two weeks
  4. Complete profiling exercises (Nsight/NCU walkthrough)

Rollout guidance and canary checks

- Phased rollout: 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% over configurable windows (default 48h)
- Canary checks (automated): p50/p95 delta, kernel-mismatch-rate, queue_time_ms, error_rate (5xx), KV_cache_hit_ratio
- Abort criteria example: p95 regression > 10% AND p99 regression > 15% OR error_rate increase > 0.1% for 5-minute window

Appendix: useful commands and snippets

- Profile a running process with Nsight (30s):
  nsys profile --output=/tmp/trace.nsys --capture-range=cudaProfilerApi --trace=cuda,osrt --duration=30s --pid <pid>

- Quick memory check:
  nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,memory.used,memory.total --format=csv -l 1

- Restart GPU agent on node: (kubectl example)
  kubectl rollout restart daemonset/gpu-agent -n runtime

- Refresh kernel profiles registry (safe operation):
  curl -X POST http://config-service.internal/api/v1/kernel-profiles/refresh -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN"

Document maintenance

- This page is reviewed quarterly by the serving-runtime team and after every major runtime release (major/minor). Add benchmark deltas and new known issues as they are discovered.
